title: High-Agency Product Management, the LNO Framework, and Strategy Memos
guest_role: Product Leader & Coach, ex-Stripe, Twitter, Google
description: Shreyas Doshi breaks down the LNO framework for time management, how to write transformative strategy memos, and the mindset of high-agency product leaders.
transcript_text:
Lenny: Welcome back to the podcast. Today I'm thrilled to have Shreyas Doshi. Shreyas, you've created some of the most widely shared frameworks in tech. One of the most impactful is the LNO Framework for task prioritization. Can you explain how it works?

Shreyas Doshi: Thanks Lenny. Most PMs suffer from chronic burnout because they treat all tasks with equal perfectionism. The LNO framework categorizes work into three distinct buckets:

1. L is for Leverage tasks: These are tasks where an exceptional 10x effort creates a 100x disproportionate return for the company. Examples include crafting the multi-year product strategy, unblocking a mission-critical architectural decision, or defining positioning. You should spend 50% of your creative energy here.
2. N is for Neutral tasks: These are standard execution tasks where doing a good, competent job is completely fine. Examples include standard sprint planning, weekly status updates, or routine user bug triage. Doing a 10x job on an N task is pure waste.
3. O is for Overhead tasks: These are low-value administrative tasks like filling out bureaucratic forms or routine expense reports. Your goal is to do them at the minimum acceptable quality as quickly as possible, or delegate/automate them.

Lenny: What separates good product strategy memos from mediocre ones?

Shreyas Doshi: A great strategy memo does not describe what you will build; it describes why the world will be different and why your company has an unfair advantage. It must clearly outline the non-goals, the explicit trade-offs you are willing to make, and what you are choosing NOT to do. If your strategy doesn't make anyone uncomfortable with what is cut, it's not a strategy—it's a wish list.

Lenny: And how do you use pre-mortems before launching high-stakes initiatives?

Shreyas Doshi: A pre-mortem is an exercise where, before writing a single line of code, the team imagines: 'It is one year in the future, and this project has failed catastrophically. What went wrong?' It gives everyone psychological safety to voice unvarnished risks that conventional optimism suppresses.
